title: Arequipa uprising over Egasa and Egesur sale
point: Plaza Mayor, central Arequipa, where a student was hit by a tear-gas canister (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Peru's January 2002 letter of intent to the IMF listed 'Privatization of the electricity generation company Egasa' as a structural benchmark due by 30 September 2002, and set asset-sale proceeds of at least US$700 million a year.

conditions: IMF letter of intent, 18 January 2002: privatizations to 'focus in the energy sector'; structural benchmarks for selling Etecen and Jorbsa (by June 2002) and Egasa (by September 2002). Egesur is not named in the letter. In November 2002 Peru told the IMF that the sale of two public firms, both program benchmarks, had been held up, and asked to change the privatization targets.

companies.name: Tractebel (Suez group)
companies.role: Sole bidder; agreed on 14 June 2002 to buy Egasa and Egesur for US$167 million

community: The sale went against a campaign promise by President Toledo not to sell the two firms. Arequipa rose up with marches, strikes and road blocks; the mayor went on hunger strike. Página/12 reported dozens injured on the first day of clashes; News & Letters reported several hundred injured. Two young men died, one of them a university student hit in the head by a police tear-gas canister. Strikes spread to Tacna, Cuzco, Puno and Moquegua; in Tacna several hundred people were arrested.
suppression: On 16 June 2002 the government declared a state of emergency and curfew in Arequipa and Tacna and sent in the armed forces. Police used tear gas against crowds.
killed_note: Página/12 (20 June 2002) names Edgar Pinto, 30, and student Fernando Talavera; News & Letters also counts two dead.
outcome: On 19 June 2002 the government agreed with Arequipa's mayors to suspend the sale until a court ruled, lifted the state of emergency and issued a public apology. The two firms were not sold to Tractebel. Peru's November 2002 letter to the IMF cut expected privatization receipts for 2002 to US$400 million.

title: Mozambique bank sales (BCM and Banco Austral)
point: Banco Austral headquarters, Avenida 25 de Setembro, Maputo (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The IMF listed the 1996 privatization of the Commercial Bank of Mozambique (BCM) among the reforms under its ESAF loan. Joseph Hanlon reports the IMF said aid would stop if the People's Development Bank (BPD) was not privatized by 30 June 1997.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: With the IMF, recommended a second sale of Banco Austral in 2001 to avoid liquidation (Mail & Guardian).

conditions: IMF press release, 24 June 1997 (second annual ESAF loan): BCM privatized in 1996; privatization program to be completed by mid-1999. BPD sale deadline of 30 June 1997 under threat of aid cuts (Hanlon, Club of Mozambique, 2024).

companies.name: Southern Bank Berhad
companies.role: Led the Malaysian–Mozambican consortium (with Frelimo-linked Invester) that bought BPD in 1997 and renamed it Banco Austral

companies.name: ABSA
companies.role: Bought 80% of Banco Austral in the 2001 re-sale

community: About US$14 million vanished from BCM before its 1996 sale. Journalist Carlos Cardoso, who was investigating that fraud, was shot dead in Maputo on 22 November 2000. At Banco Austral, the new owners piled up more than US$200 million in bad loans (Mail & Guardian); a KPMG audit found management had looted over US$40 million in three years (Hanlon). The state took the bank back in April 2001. Central-bank official António Siba-Siba Macuácua, put in charge of cleaning it up, was thrown down the stairwell of its headquarters on 11 August 2001, a day before he was due to give ABSA the bank's figures.
suppression: The Siba-Siba case was dismissed in 2009; three men were only charged in September 2024. Hanlon reports donors raised aid at the October 2001 meeting despite the unsolved killings.
killed_note: Carlos Cardoso (22 Nov 2000) and António Siba-Siba Macuácua (11 Aug 2001), per Wikipedia, Mail & Guardian and Hanlon.
outcome: ABSA took 80% of Banco Austral for about US$10–15 million in late 2001. Aníbal dos Santos was sentenced to 30 years for organizing Cardoso's murder.

title: Egypt 2016 float, fuel and fare rises
point: Central Cairo (approximate); metro fare arrests were mostly at Helwan station

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a $12 billion, three-year Extended Fund Facility on 11 November 2016 (IMF Press Release 16/501).

conditions: The IMF programme included a flexible exchange rate (adopted 3 November 2016), 'reduction of energy subsidies', a new value-added tax and 'optimization of the public sector wage bill' (IMF Press Release 16/501). About 1% of GDP was to go to food subsidies, cash transfers and social programmes.
community: The pound fell from 8.9 to about 18 per dollar; inflation reached 32.9% in April 2017; fuel prices rose by up to 55% in June 2017 (Middle East Eye). The state statistics agency CAPMAS put the share of Egyptians below the poverty line at 32.5%, up from 27.8% in 2015 (Egyptian Streets). In May 2018 Cairo metro fares rose by up to 250%, from 2 to as much as 7 pounds, for more than 3 million commuters (Al-Monitor; The New Arab).
suppression: Police arrested at least 21 people protesting the metro fare rise, most at Helwan station, according to unnamed officials (The New Arab, May 2018).
outcome: Social Solidarity Minister Ghada Waly said in 2019 that rising poverty had been predicted from the reforms and would have been twice as bad without welfare programmes (Egyptian Streets). The New Arab reported the metro rise was part of austerity tied to the IMF loan.

title: Tunisia 2018–19 public sector wage strikes
point: Tunis (approximate); the UGTT union called nationwide walkouts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a loan programme worth about $2.8 billion in December 2016. In 2017 staff called Tunisia's wage bill 'among the highest in the world' and pressed to bring it toward 12% of GDP by 2020 (IMF Press Release 17/319).

conditions: The IMF called for containing the public wage bill toward 12% of GDP by 2020 (IMF, August 2017). Reuters reported IMF pressure to freeze public sector wages and a government target of 12.5% of GDP by 2020, down from 15.5% (Al Jazeera, 2019).
community: About 650,000 public sector workers struck on 22 November 2018, closing schools, universities and ministries; hospitals ran emergency staff only (Al Jazeera; Reuters via Egypt Independent). outcome: UGTT head Noureddine Taboubi said the decision lay with the IMF, not the government. Government spokesman Iyad Dahmani said lenders including the IMF had threatened to stop financing without reforms (Reuters via Egypt Independent).

outcome: Fuel prices are now reviewed every 30 days. ActionAid Zambia called for relief on the cost of living.

title: Greece Bailout Health Spending Cap

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: One of the three troika institutions that oversaw the 2010 and 2011 bailouts (Kentikelenis et al., Lancet 2014).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other troika members; the memoranda set the health spending ceiling (Amnesty International 2020).

conditions: The memoranda with the European Commission, ECB and IMF set a target to keep 'public health expenditure at or below 6 percent of GDP' (Amnesty 2020, annex). They also required: outpatient fees (€3, raised to €5 in 2011), at least €2 billion in drug savings against 2010, hospital operating cost cuts of 10% (2011), 8% (2012) and 5% more (2013), and cuts of at least 10% in EOPYY doctors in 2012 and 10% more in 2013 (Amnesty 2020; Lancet 2014).
community: Public hospital budgets fell 26% from 2009 to 2011. New HIV infections among people who inject drugs rose from 15 (2009) to 484 (2012). Infant mortality rose 43% from 2008 to 2010; stillbirths rose 21% from 2008 to 2011; suicides rose 45% from 2007 to 2011. About 800,000 people were left without unemployment benefits or health coverage. State mental health funding fell 55% from 2011 to 2012 (Kentikelenis et al., Lancet 2014; LSHTM).
killed_note: The study reports rates (infant mortality, suicides) but no death count tied to the cuts.
outcome: Later memoranda kept the 6% target (Amnesty 2020). Amnesty's 2020 report, 'Resuscitation required', reviewed the health system after a decade of austerity. The Lancet authors note the IMF itself acknowledged deep cuts had negative economic effects.

title: Malawi fertilizer subsidy removal
point: Lilongwe District, in Malawi's central maize-growing plateau (approximate)

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Its agricultural sector credit (ASAC) capped the fertilizer subsidy at 30% in 1990/91, 25% in 1991/92 and 20% in 1992/93 (FAO). The Mail & Guardian reports the Bank pushed in the 1980s and 1990s to end fertilizer subsidies entirely.

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: A University of Washington (EPAR) review says IMF and donor pressure for fiscal austerity led Malawi in 2001 to limit free inputs to the poorest farmers.

conditions: FAO: under the ASAC credit the fertilizer subsidy could not exceed 30%, 25% and 20% in the three seasons from 1990/91, and total subsidy spending was capped at 2%, 1.6% and 1.3% of government spending. A Fertilizer Subsidy Removal Program then aimed at full removal by 1995/96. Later, under donor pressure, the universal Starter Pack of free seed and fertilizer (begun 1998) was cut back to a targeted program (Harrigan, Food Policy 2008).
community: Researchers at the University of Florida (Gough et al., 2002) found fertilizer use 'has therefore dropped significantly since 1994'; in 1999/2000 a 50 kg bag of urea cost MK 825, and prices pushed smallholders to stop or sharply cut fertilizer use. In southern Malawi 40 to 60% of rural households went short of food for two to five months a year. Free packs fell from about 3 million a year to 1.5 million in 2001 and about 1 million in 2002 (Network Ideas). FAO calls the cut in free inputs a major factor in the fall in maize output in 2001/02. After a poor 2005 harvest, almost 5 million of 13 million people needed emergency food aid (New York Times, via World Hunger Education Service); IPS reported 4.7 million facing food shortages, citing official figures.
killed_note: No death count tied to the subsidy cuts. Network Ideas cites reports of 500 to several thousand hunger deaths in 2002, a crisis also linked to the grain reserve sale (a separate card).
outcome: From 2005 the government brought back deep fertilizer subsidies against donor advice. Farmers got coupons for two 50 kg bags at about one fifth of the market price. Maize output rose from 1.2 million tonnes in 2004/05 to 2.6 million in 2005/06 and 3.2 million in 2006/07 (EPAR); good rains also helped. By 2007 Malawi was selling maize to the World Food Programme and Zimbabwe. The World Bank said it was never opposed to subsidies as such (Network Ideas).

title: Indonesia palm oil export ban lifted
point: Medan, North Sumatra, a palm oil centre where riots in early May 1998 increased panic buying (CIFOR)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: The January 15, 1998 Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies set the end of the palm oil export ban and the opening of plantations to foreign investors. CIFOR reports the IMF would not let the government bring the ban back.

conditions: IMF memorandum of January 15, 1998: the palm oil export ban to be kept only through the first quarter of 1998, then replaced by export taxes 'at rates not exceeding 20 percent'; restrictions on foreign investment in palm oil plantations removed from February 1, 1998; all other export restrictions to go within three years.
community: The government had banned crude palm oil exports to hold down cooking oil prices after the rupiah collapsed. Cooking oil rose from Rp 1,750 per kg in July 1997 to Rp 5,900 per kg in July 1998 (CIFOR, Casson 2000). The ban was replaced with export taxes of 40%, then 60% in July 1998, cut to 10% by July 1999. CIFOR warns the opening to foreign plantation investment could add pressure on forest cover; in June 1998 state forestry firms were also allowed to turn 30% of their concessions into estate crops. Communities seized back land and attacked estates in 1998; the ministry estimated at least 39,800 ha of plantations looted.
killed_note: CIFOR reports injuries and deaths in clashes between estate workers and communities in 1998 but gives no count.
outcome: CIFOR found new planting fell by a third in 1997-99 because of the crisis, so the forest effects of the foreign-investment opening were not yet clear in 2000.

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: The Bretton Woods Project and Oakland Institute say the Bank and IMF pushed creation of a land market; with the EBRD the Bank has lent $1.7 billion to the farm sector.

conditions: Pass a law ending the 2001 ban on selling farmland, plus a banking law, before a new IMF arrangement worth about $8 billion (Euronews; OSW). Parliament voted on March 30-31, 2020.
community: The law opened 41.5 million ha to sale from July 1, 2021: individuals up to 100 ha at first, and from July 2023 companies up to 10,000 ha each; a proposed 33% cap on one buyer's share of land in a local area was dropped (OSW). A February 2020 Razumkov Centre poll found only 19.6% of Ukrainians backed lifting the ban and 64.4% opposed it. The Oakland Institute says about 28% of arable land is held by oligarchs and big agribusinesses.
suppression: During the December 2019 debate, police broke up a farmers' protest outside parliament; 'dozens' were arrested (Oakland Institute).
killed_note: The Oakland Institute reports one death among protesters but gives no name or details.
outcome: The IMF approved a $5 billion Stand-By Arrangement in June 2020. Sales of state land (10.4 million ha) and sales to foreigners stayed banned (OSW).

confidence_note: The IMF condition is documented by OSW and Euronews. Harms so far are the arrests and the strong public opposition; land concentration figures come from the Oakland Institute, an advocacy group, and much of that land was leased before the law.
